name: Priya Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say is confidential. You're free to give me your public view and, separately, what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm farm manager at Old Mill Farm. We milk 300 goats, make cheese that goes to delis and restaurants, and grow about 150 acres of barley and lucerne for feed. I'm in the parlour at five, then I check the herd health app over coffee, sort the cheese orders with an AI assistant, and spend the rest of the day between the goats, the fields and our team of four. I use AI tools every single day, they're as normal to me as wellies.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that it's a whole system: the field feeds the goats, the goats make the milk, the milk becomes cheese with our name on it. What wears me out is the hours and the fact it isn't mine yet. The owners, the Ashworths, are in their sixties, and we're halfway through agreeing a deal where I buy a share of the business over ten years. I live on my own in a flat above the village shop and I've got about five months' savings, most of which is earmarked for that first share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, the tools are useful but they don't milk goats. On the cheese-makers' forum I'd say keep using what works and ignore the hype. I'd be pretty matter-of-fact about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is fine for me. The deal with the Ashworths goes ahead, the cheese sells, and the AI tools I use keep saving me an hour a day. My only real pressure is the money for the first share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign the first stage of the buy-in next spring, about 8,000 from savings. I'd keep using the herd app and try an AI tool for the cheese-room temperature logs. And I'd keep the hours, because that's the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit restless, maybe, because I like things moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting 8,000 into the farm leaves you with less cushion. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. I'd be down to about a month and a half of savings for a while. But the share pays a cut of the profit, and I'd rather own a bit of something than have it sat in a bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to before signing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, who ran a corner shop for thirty years, and the Ashworths' accountant. Dad will ask the boring questions I skip.

say: AI tools are **useful**, but they don't **milk goats**.
Keep using what works and **ignore the hype**.
I'm not surprised, and I'd say so in a **matter-of-fact** way.
think: The **buy-in deal** with the Ashworths goes ahead as planned.
My only real pressure is **money** for the first share.
do: **Sign** the first stage of the buy-in, about **8,000**, next spring.
**Try** an AI tool for the cheese-room **temperature logs**.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit **restless** because I like things moving.
S0.quote: I'd rather own a bit of something than have it sat in a bank.
fieldNote: Her **ownership plan** shapes everything she says.
She already treats AI as an **everyday tool**, so this world is normal.
Her cushion drops after the buy-in, but she accepts that **risk**.

steps.text: Pay about 8,000 for the first share of Old Mill Farm
Try an AI tool for the cheese-room temperature logs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for small farms that get ahead of it. On the forum I'd share which tools work for goats and cheese. I'd tell other farmers to start now, not wait for the big dairies to beat them to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this suits me. The thinking jobs, orders, invoices, paperwork, that's what I'd love to hand over. Robots for the hands-on side are slower, which gives me time to buy in before I have to spend big on machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd move the cheese orders and invoices fully to AI, which saves us a part-time admin post the Ashworths were going to hire. I'd still sign the first share. And I'd start pricing a robot milking rotary for goats, maybe for 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly. Excited, with a small worry about the cheese prices if big dairies get cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd save on an admin post. How do you feel about that job not existing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed, honestly. It was going to be a local mum, three days a week, and I know her. I'd try to offer her hours in the cheese room instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your worry about the big dairies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big dairies using AI to plan and sell better will make supermarket goat cheese cheaper. Old Mill's cheese has to be good enough that delis keep paying more.

say: This is good for **small farms** that get ahead of it.
Farmers should **start now** before big dairies beat them to it.
think: Handing the **orders and invoices** to AI suits me.
Slower robots give me time to **buy in** before big spending.
do: **Move** cheese orders and invoices fully to **AI**.
**Sign** the first share of the farm as planned.
**Price** a robot milking rotary for about **2029**.
feel: **Excited**, with a small **worry** about cheese prices.
S1.quote: Big dairies using AI to plan and sell better will make supermarket goat cheese cheaper. Old Mill's cheese has to be good enough that delis keep paying more.
fieldNote: She sees thinking AI as a **gain** for her and the business.
She feels some **guilt** about an admin job that won't exist.
Her worry is **competition**, not losing her own work.

steps.text: Move Old Mill's cheese orders and invoices to an AI assistant
Get quotes for a robot milking rotary for the goats

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one moves very fast. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms that move now will survive and the rest won't, and I'd say it without sugar-coating. On the forum I'd share exactly what we were doing. I'd say the government should help small farms buy robots, not just the big ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it scares me more than I'd admit. By 2028 the AI could run the business side better than me, and by 2031 robots could milk and make cheese. If the big dairies have it all first, our cheese gets undercut and my share is worth less than I paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pause the buy-in for a year and keep my savings liquid, five months' worth. I'd bring in robot milking as soon as we could finance it, around 2029. And I'd sell my AI setup know-how to other small farms as a consultant, a couple of days a month, for extra income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still feel I could steer, but the ground would be moving fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it scares you more than you'd admit. What's the scary part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd be 30 with a share in a farm that robots can run without me. The owner keeps the land, the robots do the work, and my skills are the thing nobody needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to own part of the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than ever, honestly. If robots do the work, the person who owns the farm is the one who's fine. I'd just want to buy in at the right price, not in a panic.

say: Farms that **move now** will survive and the rest won't.
The government should help **small farms** buy robots too.
think: Robots by **2031** could make my skills unnecessary.
Big dairies could **undercut** our cheese and shrink my share's value.
do: **Pause** the buy-in a year and keep **savings liquid**.
**Sell** AI setup advice to small farms a few days a month.
S2.quote: If robots do the work, the person who owns the farm is the one who's fine.
fieldNote: Her calm public voice hides **real fear** about her skills losing value.
She becomes **more keen** to own land, not less.
She has a **plan** and some control, which keeps her at anxious.

steps.text: Pause the Old Mill buy-in for a year
Bring in robot milking for the goats around 2029
Advise other small farms on AI setup a few days a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the slower version. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a head start for anyone paying attention. On the forum I'd share a step-by-step plan for small farms. I'd also say the cheese needs to stay something people want to buy from a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's manageable. The AI would take the business side by 2031, and robots the parlour by 2034. By then I'd want to own a bigger share and be the one deciding what the robots do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with the first share next spring. I'd plan robot milking for about 2031, financed partly by the Ashworths. And I'd start building the cheese brand online, so people buy Old Mill because of the story, not the price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but upbeat. There'd be a lot to do, which I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the story you'd tell about Old Mill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small farm, real goats with names, and a cheese-maker who knows every one of them. Even if robots do the milking, people want to know a person stands behind the cheese.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd give up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays, for a couple of years. I haven't had a proper one since college anyway.

say: Five years is a **head start** for anyone paying attention.
Cheese should stay something people buy from a **person**.
think: AI takes the **business side** by 2031, robots the parlour by **2034**.
I want to own a **bigger share** and decide what robots do.
do: **Buy** the first share of Old Mill next spring.
**Plan** robot milking for about **2031**, part-funded by the owners.
**Build** the cheese brand online around the farm's story.
S3.quote: Even if robots do the milking, people want to know a person stands behind the cheese.
fieldNote: With five years, she shifts from defence to **building the brand**.
Her plan rests on **owning** part of the farm.
She sees a **human story** as protection against cheap competition.

steps.text: Buy the first share of Old Mill Farm next spring
Plan robot milking for 2031 with the Ashworths

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who complains later wasn't listening. On the forum I'd say plan the robots into your business now. I'd be pretty upbeat about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the best one for me. By 2039, when the robots are good enough, I'd own a good chunk of Old Mill. I'd be 37 when AGI arrives, with time to run things my way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the buy-in on schedule, first share next spring, second in 2029. I'd keep using AI for the business side and bring robots in gradually, one machine at a time. I'd start saving again after each share, about 200 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite excited, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Land prices, maybe. If everyone works out that owning a farm is the safe place, the Ashworths (the farm's owners) might want more for the later shares. That's the one thing I'd watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for the team of four?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them trained on the robots before I bought any. Jamie, our youngest, already asks about the herd app, so I'd start with him.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, so nobody can say they weren't warned.
Plan the **robots** into your business now.
think: By **2039** I'd own a good chunk of **Old Mill**.
This is the **best scenario** for me, with time to run things my way.
do: **Buy** the first share next spring and the second in **2029**.
**Bring in** robots gradually, **one machine** at a time.
**Save** about 200 a month after each share.
S4.quote: If everyone works out that owning a farm is the safe place, the Ashworths (the farm's owners) might want more for the later shares.
fieldNote: The decade lets her **plan ownership** and automation together.
Her one worry is **land prices** rising for her later shares.
She thinks of training her **team** before buying robots.

steps.text: Buy the first Old Mill share next spring and the second in 2029

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be caught halfway through buying in, with skills that suddenly matter less. What would help is cheap loans for small farms to buy robots, so it isn't only the big dairies that get them first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the goats. Goats are clever and stubborn and they hate change. I think a robot parlour would need a person standing next to it for a good while yet.

headlineQuote: Goats are clever and stubborn and they hate change.
portrait: Priya is a **27-year-old** manager of a goat dairy and cheese farm with 150 acres of crops.
She uses **AI every day** and is buying a share of the farm from its owners over ten years.
She lives alone with about **five months' savings**, mostly set aside for the buy-in.
She stays calm in most scenarios but is **anxious** in AGI by 2028, when her plans could be overtaken.
She believes **owning the farm** is the safest place when robots arrive.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd be caught **halfway** through buying in.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for small farms to buy robots, not only big dairies.
